terms.grammar: conjunction, with the perfect indicative where English has the pluperfect
evidence: Hor. S. 2.8.57–58: postquam nihil esse perīclī sēnsimus, ērigimur
Verg. A. 1.216: postquam exēmpta famēs epulīs mēnsaeque remōtae
terms.comment: “After he had come” is postquam vēnit: Latin uses the perfect, as with ubi and ut. Written apart with a measure of time: post … quam, so many days after.

terms.grammar: a noun and a participle in the ablative
evidence: Varr. RR 3.16.35: quō factō nōn modo dēsistunt pugnā
terms.comment: The usual Latin for “after doing X” or “when X was done”, with no conjunction: quō factō, after which; cēnā factā, after dinner. Lewis & Short has the grammarians’ ablātīvus; the name of the construction is modern.

phrases.latin: postquam nihil esse perīclī sēnsimus, ērigimur
phrases.english: once we see there is no danger, we sit up again

phrases.latin: postquam exēmpta famēs epulīs mēnsaeque remōtae
phrases.english: after hunger was taken away by the feast and the tables removed

phrases.latin: haec postquam omnia sēcrēvimus, tum suō quaeque locō disposuimus
phrases.english: after we had sorted all these things, we put each in its place

phrases.latin: quae crēbrius inter sē pugnābunt, aspargī eās oportet aquā mulsā. quō factō nōn modo dēsistunt pugnā, sed etiam conferciunt sē lingentēs
phrases.english: the bees that keep fighting should be sprinkled with honey-water; after that they not only stop fighting but crowd together licking one another
